events.title: Naxalbari Uprising – The Spark
events.description: A land dispute between tribal farmer Bimal Kisan and landlord Ishwar Tirkey escalates. On 24–25 May, police fire on protesters, killing 8 villagers including 2 children. The uprising, led by local commanders and communist ideologues, marks the birth of the Naxalite movement.
source_fact_ids: fact: Naxalite movement originated in the late 1960s in Naxalbari village
fact: The immediate trigger was a land dispute between Bimal Kisan and Ishwar Tirkey
fact: On 24-25 May 1967, police firing killed 8 villagers

events.title: CPI(ML) Formation – Armed Revolution Declared
events.description: Charu Majumdar founds the Communist Party of India (Marxist-Leninist) to wage an armed revolution. The party adopts the ‘annihilation of class enemies’ as its guiding principle.
events.location: Nationwide, ideological base in West Bengal
source_fact_ids: fact: CPI-ML was formed on 22 April 1969, with Charu Majumdar as its leader, advocating armed revolution

events.title: Operation Steeplechase – Crushing the First Wave
events.description: Massive police and army operation arrests hundreds of Naxalites across West Bengal. Leader Charu Majumdar is captured on 16 July 1972 and dies in custody on 28 July, dealing a fatal blow to the movement.
source_fact_ids: fact: Charu Majumdar was arrested on 16 July 1972 and died in police custody on 28 July 1972
fact: Operation Steeplechase (1971-1972) led to capture of Charu Majumdar

events.title: Emergency Crackdown – MISA Unleashed
events.description: Prime Minister Indira Gandhi uses the Maintenance of Internal Security Act (MISA) to arrest thousands of Naxalites. The movement is virtually decapitated.
events.location: Pan-India, especially West Bengal and Andhra Pradesh
source_fact_ids: fact: During the Emergency (1975-77), Indira Gandhi used MISA to crack down on Naxalites

events.title: Release and Betrayal – Naxalites Walk Free
events.description: Prime Minister Morarji Desai releases many Naxal prisoners who renounce violence. Many later rejoin the armed struggle, setting the stage for revival.
source_fact_ids: fact: In 1977, PM Morarji Desai released many Naxal prisoners who renounced violence

events.title: People’s War Group (PWG) – The Resurgence
events.description: Kondapalli Seetharamaiah, released from jail, regroups Naxal factions and founds the People’s War Group in Andhra Pradesh. The insurgency gets a second life.
source_fact_ids: fact: Kondapalli Seetharamaiah, released from jail, regrouped Naxal factions and formed PWG in 1980

events.title: Fragmented Resistance – PWG, MCC, and the Build‑up
events.description: Multiple Maoist groups operate independently across the heartland. They forge links with LTTE and ULFA for training and arms, expand tribal support bases, and perfect guerrilla tactics.
source_fact_ids: fact: Naxalites and LTTE had training and arms supply relations in 1990s
fact: Naxalites and ULFA had coordination and tactical exchange
fact: Weaponry commonly used includes looted AK-47s, INSAS, UBGL, RPG, IEDs

events.title: CPI (Maoist) – A Unified Front
events.description: The merger of the People’s War Group and the Maoist Communist Centre gives birth to the Communist Party of India (Maoist). A unified command escalates the conflict dramatically.
events.location: Nationwide, headquartered in the Red Corridor
source_fact_ids: fact: The CPI (Maoist) was formed in 2004 through the merger of PWG and MCC

events.title: Salwa Judum – State‑Sponsored Vigilanteism
events.description: Congress leader Mahendra Karma launches Salwa Judum in Chhattisgarh, arming tribal youth to fight Maoists. The militia is later banned by the Supreme Court in 2011 for horrific human rights abuses, alienating locals.
source_fact_ids: fact: Salwa Judum movement, launched in 2005 by Mahendra Karma, armed tribal youth; banned by Supreme Court in 2011 due to human rights violations

events.title: Peak Maoist Dominance – The Red Corridor
events.description: Maoist influence extends to over 180 districts across 10 states covering 92,000 sq km. The ‘Red Corridor’ becomes a zone of parallel governance.
events.location: Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Odisha, Bihar, West Bengal, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Maharashtra, MP, Karnataka
source_fact_ids: fact: At its peak around 2005-2010, Maoist influence extended to over 180 districts across 10 states, covering approximately 92,000 sq km
fact: The Red Corridor refers to the contiguous region affected by Naxalism

events.title: Dantewada Ambush – India’s Darkest Day Against Naxals
events.description: A CRPF convoy is ambushed in the Mukrana forest. 76 security personnel are killed in the deadliest Maoist attack in India’s history, demonstrating the insurgents’ deadly capability.
source_fact_ids: fact: On 6 April 2010, in Dantewada, a CRPF convoy was ambushed, resulting in the death of 76 security personnel
fact: Naxal commander Hidma orchestrated multiple major attacks

events.title: Operation Green Hunt – Full‑Scale War
events.description: The Indian government launches a nationwide offensive involving CRPF and state police to break the Maoist stronghold. Encounters, smart weapons, and intelligence operations intensify.
events.location: Red Corridor, especially Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Odisha
source_fact_ids: fact: Operation Green Hunt (2009 onwards) - Nationwide offensive by CRPF and state police against Maoists
fact: The security forces now employ helicopters, drones, thermal imaging

events.title: Darbha Valley Ambush – Congress Leadership Decapitated
events.description: Maoists ambush a Congress rally in Darbha Valley, killing Salwa Judum founder Mahendra Karma and several other Congress leaders. A high‑profile assassination that shocks the nation.
source_fact_ids: fact: Mahendra Karma, founder of Salwa Judum, was killed by Maoists in 2013 Darbha Valley ambush

events.title: SAMADHAN – The 8‑Point Masterstroke
events.description: The BJP government adopts the ‘Samadhan’ strategy: Smart leadership, Aggressive strategy, Motivation and training, Dashboard‑based monitoring, Harnessing technology, Action plan for each threat, No access to financing. It marks a coordinated, holistic push against Maoism.
events.location: Nationwide policy, field implementation in LWE districts
source_fact_ids: fact: In 2017, the BJP government launched the 'Samadhan' strategy, an eight-point plan

events.title: Massive Shrinkage of the Red Corridor
events.description: Maoist-affected districts plummet from 126 in 2013 to 38 in 2024. Attacks decline from 2,258 in 2009 to 349 by August 2021. Government claims steady progress.
source_fact_ids: fact: Recent operations have reduced Maoist-affected districts from 126 in 2013 to 38 in 2024, and attacks declined

events.title: Shahid Minar in the Shadow of Camps
events.description: Despite security camps, Maoists erect a 60‑ft martyrs’ column in Bijapur district; 10,000 people attend the gathering, showcasing enduring tribal support.
source_fact_ids: fact: a 60-ft 'Shahid Minar' built near security camps in Bijapur district in 2022 attended by 10,000 people

events.title: Amit Shah’s Deadline – Naxalism Eradicated
events.description: Home Minister Amit Shah declares that Naxalism will be completely eradicated by 31 March 2026. The countdown begins.
source_fact_ids: fact: Home Minister Amit Shah declared that Naxalism will be completely eradicated by 31 March 2026

events.title: Unfinished War – Ideology vs. Development
events.description: While territory shrinks, the ‘Urban Naxal’ network, unaddressed tribal land rights, and corporate mining tensions keep the ideological embers glowing. The final chapter remains unwritten.
events.location: Red Corridor remnants and urban centers
source_fact_ids: fact: The 'Urban Naxal' phenomenon refers to ideological supporters within cities
unknown: Impact of corporate mining on local tribal support for Maoists
unknown: Effect of surrender and rehabilitation programs

master_narrative_arc: From a bullet‑riddled village in 1967 Bengal, a grass‑roots peasant uprising mutates into India’s longest‑running armed rebellion. The documentary traces how a land dispute sparked an ideology‑driven insurgency, outlasting the execution of its founders, the iron fist of the Emergency, and decades of military campaigns. After near‑extinction, a furtive rebuilding produced the People’s War Group and later the unified CPI (Maoist), which by 2010 held a ‘Red Corridor’ larger than many countries. The 2010 Dantewada ambush—76 CRPF men dead—showed the state’s ultimate vulnerability, but also triggered a ruthless, tech‑backed counter‑offensive. Salwa Judum, Green Hunt, and the SAMADHAN strategy together shrank Maoist territory to a fraction of its peak. Yet, as the government sets a 2026 finish line, a clandestine martyrs’ pillar, shadowy urban supporters, and unresolved tribal land grievances whisper that the war may end in the jungle but not in the hearts of the dispossessed. The film questions whether a purely security‑driven victory can ever extinguish a fire lit by deep socio‑economic inequality.
